prompt_text:
The figure summarizes how T cells are regulated in lymph nodes and tumors, and how different antibody designs try to restore anti-tumor activity. Overall, it contrasts normal co-stimulation during T-cell priming with the suppressed signaling typical of the tumor microenvironment, then shows therapeutic strategies that reintroduce activation signals.

In the lymph node, a T cell receives signal 1 through TCR recognition of antigen on MHC and signal 2 through CD28 binding to CD80/CD86, leading to activation and proliferation. This is restrained by inhibitory checkpoints such as PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4. In tumors, the T cell appears to encounter antigen but lacks proper co-stimulatory input, so effector function is limited and checkpoint inhibition dominates.

The lower panels compare treatment concepts. Conventional checkpoint inhibitors block PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4, allowing endogenous stimulatory signaling to recover. By contrast, tumor-associated antigen (TAA)-targeted bispecific antibodies actively provide activation: one format links TAA to CD28 to deliver signal 2, another links TAA to CD3 to provide signal 1, and these can be combined. A related strategy pairs a TAA×CD28 bispecific with immune checkpoint blockade. Finally, a trispecific antibody appears to engage TAA, CD28, and CD3 simultaneously, inducing both signals together to drive T-cell activation, proliferation, and effector function.
